blocks.text: 概述

inlines.text: 概述
我们测量什么。
AI 有望加速科学发现，但加速幅度取决于 AI 能做什么，以及科学家如何使用它。我们采用隐私保护方法，研究了 207,000 个 Claude 和 Claude Code 科研会话，以了解 Claude 在各科学领域和研究任务中的使用情况。我们开展这项研究，是为了帮助公众更好地了解当今 AI 在科学领域的现状，并评估 AI 未来可能对科学发现产生的影响。
科学家在哪些领域使用 Claude。

相对于各领域的研究人员数量，Claude 在形式科学领域（如计算机科学、数学和统计学）使用更多，在健康和基于实验室的物理科学领域使用较少。科学家主要用 Claude 分析数据和写作。仅数据分析一项就占 Claude 会话的约三分之一，占 Claude Code 会话的近一半。科学家较少用它来生成想法和收集数据，尽管在一项配套调查中，他们将这些任务列为对科学发现最重要的任务。不过，专为科研工作设计的专用 AI 工具可能缩小科学家实际使用 AI 的研究任务与他们视为最重要的任务之间的差距。例如，在 Claude Science 上，想法生成所占的使用比例约为 Claude 上的两倍。
Claude 的使用如何反映 AI 能力。

我们构建了一个衡量指标，用来评估 AI 在理论上能多好地完成每项研究任务。AI 最适合的任务（在该指标上排名前 20%）获得的 Claude 使用量，是研究人员投入这些任务的时间所预测的两到四倍。AI 最不适合的任务（排名后 20%），包括大多数体力工作，获得的 Claude 使用量非常少。我们在各领域观察到同样的模式：AI 能出色完成许多任务的领域，如计算机科学和统计学，使用 Claude 更多。
这对科学发现速度可能意味着什么。

我们用一个简单模型探索了 AI 可能以多大幅度加速研究的几种情景。如果现有的 AI 能力得到广泛采用，它们可能使某些领域的研究产出翻倍。如果 AI 能承担所有非体力研究工作，计算机科学和统计学等领域的产出可能提高多达 15 倍，而化学和生物学等受物理瓶颈制约的实验科学领域，产出将提高三到四倍。在我们对积极使用 AI 的研究人员的调查中，约 40% 预计到 2030 年 AI 模型将能自行开展完整的研究项目。

inlines.text: 引言

blocks.text: 科学曾被描述为“无尽的前沿”（Bush 1945）。但历史上，我们探索这一前沿的速度受限于一种稀缺资源：人类研究者的时间和才华。人工智能可以通过放大研究人员的能力来缓解这一限制，同时改变发现的过程和探索的速度（Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024）。很少有 AI 应用能比这更关乎人类福祉。鉴于研究相比大多数经济部门具有高度认知属性，AI 在这一领域的影响可能尤其大、来得尤其早。

blocks.text: 近期的一些例子显示，AI 在科学发现中扮演着越来越重要的角色。在结构生物学领域，AlphaFold 预测了超过 2 亿个蛋白质的三维结构（Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024），其研发者分享了 2024 年诺贝尔化学奖。在材料科学领域，GNoME 预测了 38 万种稳定的新晶体（Merchant et al. 2023）。在数学领域，研究人员借助 AI 系统帮助解决悬置数十年的 Erdős 问题、为一个千禧年大奖难题给出潜在证明，并在其他重大问题上取得进展，从公开猜想一直到验证里程碑式的证明（Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026）。

blocks.text: 更快的科学发现固然能给人类带来巨大益处，但 AI 驱动的研究也伴随着风险和不确定性。人类监督减少，可能导致有人去追求危险或不道德的研究。AI 还可能重塑研究人员的职业生涯，使研究工作变得更有或更缺乏回报，并改变人类追求知识这一事业所承载的意义感。

blocks.text: 这项研究的目标是衡量科学家使用 Claude 的不同方式，同时保护他们工作内容的细节。为此，我们采用保护隐私的基础设施，分析消费者方案中 Claude 的科研使用情况。我们用一个语言模型充当“分类器”，读取每段会话记录，并按照预定义分类体系（Alamos 与 Althoff 2026 提出的 SciNet 分类法）为其打上一组固定类别的标签，例如所属领域和涉及的研究任务。研究团队为本报告保留和分析的，只有这些标签（如“化学”或“数据清洗”），不涉及对话中的其他信息。本研究使用的分类器都不会提取或存储开放式信息，也不会记录研究内容细节，例如研究数据集、假设、实验方法、早期发现或未发表论文。结果仅以汇总形式报告，且只针对达到最低不同账户数门槛的单元格。本研究引入的所有分类器见附录。

blocks.text: 我们的测量分两步进行。第一个分类器判断一段会话记录是否涉及科研工作。第二个分类器再把每段此类记录归入 SciNet 分类法中的领域、子领域和任务。SciNet 包含 7,262 项任务，覆盖 34 个领域和 318 个子领域。分类法中的部分任务（如撰写论文稿件）是所有领域共有的，另一些则只属于特定领域或子领域。例如，在分类法中，预测光吸收和发射光谱这一任务就专属于材料科学。这些任务合在一起，覆盖了产出新研究发现的全过程。

blocks.text: 除了了解哪些领域在使用 Claude，我们还希望弄清科学家用它来做什么。研究工作涉及许多不同的任务，从提出假设、分析数据，到撰写研究论文。为了更好地了解 Claude 如何支持科学发现，我们研究了使用情况在这些任务之间的差异。为此，我们把每个会话归入 SciNet 的 7,262 项任务之一。这些任务有些是所有领域通用的，比如起草稿件；有些则针对特定领域或子领域，比如通过差异基因表达分析比较肿瘤亚型，这属于癌症生物学。该分类体系区分了研究任务与非研究任务：前者是研究人员为产出新的科学发现而执行的任务，后者则包括教学、同行评审以及为院系或领域提供的服务。5 我们的分析仅限于涵盖八个类别的研究任务：(1) 数据分析，(2) 写作与沟通，(3) 数据收集，(4) 阅读与知识获取，(5) 理论分析，(6) 设计与开发（软件、材料和创意作品），(7) 构思与假设生成，以及 (8) 其他，例如研究管理。

inlines.text: 使用方式与能力的关系

blocks.text: AI 的使用情况是否与 AI 能力同步？领域规模能解释 Claude 使用差异的一部分，但并非全部。例如，计算机科学领域的研究者使用 Claude 的程度远超该领域规模所能预测的水平，而营养学领域的研究者则用得少得多。同样，研究者把自身时间花在哪里，也不能完全预测他们最常在哪些环节使用 Claude。数据分析、写作等大类任务的使用占比远高于其研究时间占比，而数据收集、构思与假设生成等任务的使用占比则小得多。在此，我们检验这些使用差异是否反映了 AI 实际具备的能力。

inlines.text: AI 的使用情况是否与 AI 能力同步？领域规模能解释 Claude 使用差异的一部分，但并非全部。例如，计算机科学领域的研究者使用 Claude 的程度远超该领域规模所能预测的水平，而营养学领域的研究者则用得少得多。同样，研究者把自身时间花在哪里，也不能完全预测他们最常在哪些环节使用 Claude。数据分析、写作等大类任务的使用占比远高于其研究时间占比，而数据收集、构思与假设生成等任务的使用占比则小得多。在此，我们检验这些使用差异是否反映了 AI 实际具备的能力。

blocks.text: 为衡量特定任务上的 AI 能力，我们先用大语言模型分类器构建能力评分。对于每项任务，SciNet 都列出了科学家完成任务所需执行的各个步骤。例如，化学中有一项任务涉及纯化反应混合物，而该任务的一个步骤是装填色谱柱。分类器会看到分类体系中成对的步骤，并被问及 AI 更能胜任哪一个。我们用 Bradley–Terry 模型汇总这些比较结果——国际象棋选手的 Elo 评分正是基于这一模型，依据两两对局结果进行排名。某个步骤在比较中获胜，得分就上升；落败则下降。随后我们对每项任务各步骤的得分取平均，得到任务级评分（详见附录）。我们将这一指标称为理论 AI 能力，将某项任务的具体得分称为其AI 能力评分。

blocks.text: 先看 RL 适用性。在强化学习中，AI 模型会反复尝试一项任务，成功时获得奖励，从而学会如何完成该任务。当成功易于验证、可以在计算环境中模拟大量示例、并且反馈能够快速给出时，任务就特别适合 RL（Lambert et al. 2024；Guo et al. 2025）。我们使用 SciNet 中针对这三个 RL 相关组件的任务级指标，并将它们汇总为一个指数。任务的能力评分与其 RL 指数评分高度相关（相关系数为 0.78），而后者是单独分类的。这表明，AI 在最容易应用 RL 的研究任务上能力最强。

inlines.text: AI 驱动的研究加速情景

blocks.text: 科学技术进步的速度取决于好的想法以及实现这些想法的手段。从历史上看，两者都受限于人的能力。研究者数量有限，每个人用于提出假设、设计合适的实验、运行分析并综合研究结果的时间也有限。

inlines.text: 科学技术进步的速度取决于好的想法以及实现这些想法的手段。从历史上看，两者都受限于人的能力。研究者数量有限，每个人用于提出假设、设计合适的实验、运行分析并综合研究结果的时间也有限。

blocks.text: AI 可以通过两种方式缓解这些限制。第一，它可以承担研究者目前所做的工作，让他们能够探索更多想法。第二，它可以贡献研究者原本可能想不到的想法。第二种方式最终可能最为重要，但更难衡量，因此我们的分析聚焦于第一种。

blocks.text: 我们考察了 AI 推动科学加速的三种情景。情景 1 假设当前 AI 能力得到广泛采用，这一假设基于我们的调查和 AI 能力评分估算得出。情景 2 和情景 3 是假设的未来情形：AI 将 75% 或 100% 的非物理研究步骤完全自动化——这些步骤是 SciNet 中构成每项研究任务的各个具体动作——并从 AI 能力评分最高的步骤开始。在三种情景中，研究者都继续执行物理步骤。这些情景仅作示例，并非预测。它们展示了物理工作、理论 AI 能力和 AI 成本可能如何影响科学研究的加速，以及哪些领域可能加速最快。

blocks.text: 针对每个场景，我们报告两项指标。第一项是AI 占比：在一项研究中，AI 可以承担的研究人员时间比例。考虑到研究人员目前的时间分配方式，它衡量的是 AI 能释放出多少人类研究时间，这一指标直接来自我们上面的分析。研究人员可以把释放出来的时间转投其他工作，从而提高研究产出。第二项指标是加速倍数，用来估算这种增益：在固定研究预算下，研究产出相对于没有 AI 时的增长幅度。它告诉我们，同样的预算能多产出多少研究成果。释放出的时间并不会一比一地转化为更多产出，一方面是因为研究人员会把精力转向 AI 帮助较小的任务，另一方面是因为 AI 本身也有成本。

inlines.text: 场景 1：当前能力

blocks.text: 以现有能力，如果AI得到广泛采用，它可以承担完成一项新研究所需研究者时间的27%–52%，各学科中位数为38%（图13左图）。这些比例意味着研究加速幅度从艺术学科的1.35倍、人类学的1.36倍、化学的1.41倍，到计算机科学的1.96倍和统计学的2.02倍不等（图13右图）。加速幅度之所以有限，是因为如今的AI工作大多是辅助性或分担性的，而非自主完成，研究者仍然要在几乎每个环节上投入大量时间。即便是AI就绪度最高的领域——其工作几乎完全是认知性的——加速幅度也只有约2倍。这些估算的前提是AI广泛普及，且研究者将其应用于当前所有有用的环节。

blocks.text: 学科间的差异主要由两个因素解释。第一个是体力工作，没有物理层面的集成，AI无法承担这类工作。在农业科学、生物医学科学、化学和材料科学等实验室与野外科学中，38%–41%的研究者时间花在体力环节上，而各学科中位数仅为4%。仅体力工作占比这一项，就能解释AI占比差异的约三分之一。第二个因素是认知工作中AI能力评分的分布。艺术和歷史花在体力环节上的时间很少（分别为10%和4%），但其认知环节的AI能力评分较低，或许是因为定性和解释性工作不太适合强化学习。相比之下，计算机科学和统计学的评分高、AI占比大，这主要得益于数据分析——这是各学科中AI能力评分最高的一类工作。

inlines.text: 情景2和情景3：更高程度的自动化

blocks.text: 这两个更具推测性的情景高度依赖对AI覆盖范围和成本的假设。在它们之中，更高程度的自动化会大幅提升AI占比和加速幅度，并拉大学科之间的差距。

inlines.text: 这两个更具推测性的情景高度依赖对AI覆盖范围和成本的假设。在它们之中，更高程度的自动化会大幅提升AI占比和加速幅度，并拉大学科之间的差距。

blocks.text: 在情景2中，75%的非体力环节可由AI完成，加速幅度在计算机科学达到约8倍，统计学和图书馆与信息科学约7倍，经济学约6倍。大多数其他社会科学、数学、物理学和天文学达到4–5倍，而实验室科学和医学科学约为2–3倍。实验室科学以及艺术与人文学科获益最少，但原因各不相同。在实验室科学中，大量工作是体力性的，仍须由研究者完成。在艺术与人文学科中，工作大多是认知性的，但AI能力评分较低，因此被自动化的环节很少。在计算机科学中，自动化环节占非体力研究者时间的82%，而在艺术学科中仅占28%。历史学、人类学和艺术的加速幅度约为2倍或更低。

blocks.text: 在情景3中，艺术与人文学科走在前列，而实验科学则依然受到制约。一旦AI将所有非物理步骤自动化，较低的AI能力评分便不再限制认知工作，AI可以在许多领域承担几乎全部研究工作（图13左侧面板）。在这一推测性情景中，物理任务较少的领域——包括统计学、计算机科学、经济学、数学、心理学以及大部分社会科学和艺术与人文学科——达到约15–16倍。而实验室或实地工作较多的领域，如生物学、化学、材料科学、农业科学和生物医学科学，仅达到3–4倍。在缺乏自动化实验室的情况下，这些领域约占总研究时间40%的物理步骤仍然是瓶颈。

blocks.text: 这些情景带来两点启示。第一，物理瓶颈依然强大。AI在没有物理集成的情况下无法执行的步骤，会占据研究者的时间和预算，从而限制加速幅度。第二，在不存在此类瓶颈的地方，非凡的进展速度成为可能，而AI的成本则成为限制因素。在我们的假设下，一项由AI完全自动化的任务，其成本仍约为研究者亲自执行成本的十六分之一，因此加速幅度接近约16倍并止步于此。更低的AI成本会按比例提高这一上限，例如，将AI成本减半，进展速度就会翻倍。如果成本大幅下降，包括AI日后自动化的更难任务，那么没有物理瓶颈的领域可能会加速到远超这些估计的水平。

blocks.text: 研究者的预期

inlines.text: 研究者的预期

blocks.text: 上述情景描述了一系列可能性。研究者自身的预期可以基于专业知识提供独特的指引。为了收集他们的观点，我们对生命与健康科学领域研究者的调查询问了他们预计AI独立工作时，何时能在不同类别的科研工作上匹敌其领域内最优秀的研究者（图15）。受访者的近期预期很高：超过一半预计AI到2027年在数据分析上能匹敌顶尖研究者，38%表示AI已经达到这一水平。到2030年，94%预计AI将在数据分析上匹敌最优秀的研究者，89%在写作上，72%在构思和数据收集上。对构思和数据收集的预期较低，这与目前Claude在这些任务上的使用较少相一致。

blocks.text: 对于无需人类介入的端到端 AI 研究，人们的预期更为保守，但研究者仍预计会有显著进展。约 40% 的受访者认为到 2030 年 AI 能独立完成完整的研究项目，约 64% 认为到 2035 年可以实现，不过有 16% 的人认为这永远不会发生。对于 AI 自主产出科学突破，预期则更为谨慎：约半数研究者认为这要到 2035 年之后才可能实现，甚至永远无法实现。总体来看，许多研究者预计未来十年自动化水平会很高，这与我们更激进的自动化情景大体一致。这些预期能以多快的速度、在多大程度上成为现实，不仅取决于 AI 作为软件技术的进步，也取决于能否建成克服物理障碍的自动化实验室。

blocks.text: 讨论

inlines.text: 讨论

blocks.text: 如果 AI 能帮助加快科学发现，就可能有助于提高生活水平、加快疾病治疗的进展。我们的估算表明，潜在收益相当可观。但 AI 研究能力的提升并不会自动转化为快速进展；能否实现这种加速，还取决于我们如何应对若干制约因素。

inlines.text: 如果 AI 能帮助加快科学发现，就可能有助于提高生活水平、加快疾病治疗的进展。我们的估算表明，潜在收益相当可观。但 AI 研究能力的提升并不会自动转化为快速进展；能否实现这种加速，还取决于我们如何应对若干制约因素。

blocks.text: 首先，采用速度可能大幅滞后于能力。新技术的扩散通常很慢（Comin and Hobijn 2010），而生产率的提升往往要等到组织围绕新技术完成重组之后才会显现（David 1990; Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson 2021）。个体的学习过程、组织或系统层面的摩擦，以及 AI 获取或基础设施方面的限制，都可能拖慢采用速度。

blocks.text: 其次，研究可能仍会面临 AI 无法消除的瓶颈。物理实验成本高、速度慢，即便 AI 能力极强，也可能大幅限制进展。在上文的情景中，我们在实验台科学领域尤其能看到这一点。选择研究什么可能是另一个瓶颈。研究问题在很大程度上决定了一个研究项目的价值，而 AI 能否提出好问题仍不清楚。如果构思环节是瓶颈，那么即便回答某个特定问题变得便宜得多，加速也会受到限制。反过来，如果 AI 在提出高质量假设方面超越人类，加速可能更为显著，尤其是在检验假设成本高昂的领域。

blocks.text: 第三，AI 赋能的研究可能提升研究产出的数量或质量，而这两者对科学的影响并不相同。新论文激增可以加速一个领域的发展，但也可能超出科学家吸收或验证成果的能力。另一方面，从显微镜、望远镜到统计软件，新技术在历史上一直提升了科学洞见的质量，AI 同样可以让更全面的分析和更宏大的项目变得可行。而随着论文生产变得更容易，研究界可能越来越奖励那些特别新颖或高质量的工作。更高效的研究究竟带来更多数量还是更高质量，取决于研究者的选择，以及期刊、资助方和机构设定的激励。

blocks.text: 第四，研究的组织方式可能以难以预料的方式发生变化。随着 AI 能力更强、自主性更高，AI 系统可能主导验证、审稿和重要成果的传播，从而缓解上述的吸收问题。更远的未来，AI 研究智能体还可能借助机器人和自动化实验室，组成自己的大型社群，独立于人类推进科学前沿。这种自主的 AI 研究将带来一系列问题：人类如何跟踪新知识、能否理解这些知识，以及知识是如何产生的。

blocks.text: 第五，更自主的 AI 系统可能加大一项挑战：确保 AI 驱动的研究始终与人类目标保持一致。随着 AI 智能体变得更强、更有创造力，让人类参与关键的研究决策——比如研究哪些问题、如何研究——可能对安全和人类福祉至关重要。科学发现本身，或研究的副产品，也可能带来风险，尤其是在生物学领域：加速医学进步的能力，同样可能产生危险的知识或材料。在这种情况下，可能有必要在研究过程中设置刻意的检查点，这意味着我们要接受更慢的进展以降低风险。

blocks.text: 最后，研究者所从事的工作可能发生显著变化。一个影响可能是研究者工作满意度的变化。如果 AI 接管了令人愉快或有成就感的工作，满意度可能下降，选择科研职业的人也会减少。如果 AI 接管的是研究者觉得枯燥的工作，满意度则可能上升。行政事务就是一个潜在目标。在美国，联邦资助项目的主要研究者报告称，约 44% 的研究时间花在满足行政要求而非做研究上（Schneider et al. 2020），减轻这一负担可能带来巨大好处，既节省时间，又提升整体满意度。归根结底，净效应并不确定，并且可能随 AI 能力的演进而变化。一种乐观的看法是，AI 将拓展发现的机会，而这正是科研职业令人满足的核心所在。如果科学是一场驶向“无尽前沿”的航行，AI 或许是一艘新船，让研究者能在广阔的研究问题与发现之海中走得更远。

blocks.text: Summary

inlines.text: Summary
What we measure.

AI could speed up scientific discovery, but how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future.
Where scientists use Claude.

Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude.
How Claude use tracks AI capability.

We create a measure of how well AI can, in theory, perform each research task. The tasks AI is best suited to (the top 20% on this measure) get two to four times as much Claude use as the time researchers spend on them would predict. The tasks AI is least suited to (the bottom 20%), which include most physical work, get very little. We observe the same pattern across fields: fields where AI can perform many tasks well, such as computer science and statistics, use Claude more.
What this could mean for the speed of scientific discovery.

Using a simple model, we explore scenarios for how much AI could speed up research. If existing AI capabilities are widely adopted, they could double research output in some fields. If AI could carry out all non-physical research work, output in fields such as computer science and statistics could rise as much as 15-fold, while output in bench sciences such as chemistry and biology, which are held back by physical bottlenecks, would rise three- or fourfold. In our survey of researchers who actively use AI, about 40% expect AI models to carry out full research projects on their own by 2030.

blocks.text: Introduction

inlines.text: Introduction

blocks.text: Science has been described as an “endless frontier” (Bush 1945). But how fast we explore that frontier has historically been limited by a scarce resource: the time and talent of human researchers. Artificial intelligence could ease that limit by amplifying what researchers can do, transforming both the process of discovery and the pace of exploration (Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024). Few applications of AI could matter more for human welfare. Given the highly cognitive nature of research compared with most sectors of the economy, AI’s effects may be particularly large and early in this domain.

blocks.text: Recent examples show AI playing a growing role in scientific discovery. In structural biology, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional shapes of over 200 million proteins (Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024), and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In materials science, GNoME predicted 380,000 stable new crystals (Merchant et al. 2023). In mathematics, researchers have used AI systems to help resolve decades-old Erdős problems, produce a potential proof for a Millennium Prize problem, and make progress on other major problems, from open conjectures to verifying landmark proofs (Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026).

blocks.text: How we conducted this research

inlines.text: How we conducted this research

blocks.text: Our goal with this research is to measure the different ways scientists use Claude while protecting the details of their work. To do this, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to analyze the scientific use of Claude on consumer plans. A language model, used here as a “classifier,” reads each session transcript and labels it with a fixed set of categories, such as the field and the research task it involves, according to a predefined taxonomy (SciNet taxonomy by Alamos and Althoff 2026). The resulting labels, such as “chemistry” or “data cleaning,” are the only information from these conversations retained and analyzed by the research team for this report. No classifier employed in this study extracts and stores open-ended information or details on research content, such as research datasets, hypotheses, experimental methods, early findings, or unpublished papers. Results are reported only in aggregate and only for cells that meet a minimum number of distinct accounts. All classifiers introduced in this study are listed in the Appendix.

blocks.text: Our measurement involves two steps. A first classifier identifies whether a session transcript involves scientific work. A second classifier then assigns each of these transcripts to a field, subfield, and task in the SciNet taxonomy. SciNet contains 7,262 tasks, spanning 34 fields and 318 subfields. inlines.text: How Claude use varies across scientific fields

blocks.text: We begin by describing how Claude use varies across scientific fields. Figure 1 compares a field’s share of sessions against the share of global researchers in that field, giving us a sense of relative use per scientific field.1 On Claude, the three largest fields by session share are computer science (11.9%), engineering (8.4%), and medicine (7.7%), which are also among the largest fields by global researcher counts.2 Overall, fields with a larger share of researchers also tend to account for a larger share of Claude sessions (log-log correlation of 0.79).

blocks.text: How Claude use varies across research tasks

inlines.text: How Claude use varies across research tasks

blocks.text: Beyond understanding which fields use Claude, we also want to understand what scientists use it for. Research involves many different tasks, from generating hypotheses and analyzing data to writing up findings in a research paper. To better discern how Claude supports scientific discovery, we study how usage varies across these tasks. To do so, we assign each session to one of the 7,262 tasks in SciNet. These tasks can be universal to all fields, such as drafting manuscripts, or specific to fields or subfields, such as performing differential gene expression analysis to compare tumor subtypes, which is associated with cancer biology. The taxonomy distinguishes between research tasks, which researchers perform to produce new scientific findings, and non-research tasks, such as teaching, peer review, and service to the department or field.5 We limit our analysis to research tasks spanning eight categories: (1) data analysis, (2) writing and communication, (3) data gathering, (4) reading and knowledge acquisition, (5) theoretical analysis, (6) design and development (of software, materials, and creative works), (7) ideation and hypothesis generation, and (8) other, such as administering research.

blocks.text: For each task category, we calculate its share of Claude and Claude Code sessions separately. To assess whether usage in a category is high or low, we consider the share of their time that researchers typically spend on that category, as estimated by SciNet. This provides a benchmark to assess whether the share of Claude use across different task categories follows or deviates from how researchers spend their time.

blocks.text: Usage by task category. Data analysis tasks have the highest usage in absolute terms and are overrepresented relative to researcher time. Data analysis accounts for 33.7% of sessions on Claude and 48.1% on Claude Code, compared with 27.6% of researcher time. Writing and communication tasks also show high usage, especially on Claude (32.0%, compared with 16.0% of researcher time).6 Data gathering tasks have low relative usage, accounting for 28.6% of researcher time but only 11.5% of sessions on Claude and 11.9% on Claude Code. The underrepresentation of data gathering is particularly strong for tasks with physical barriers, such as the collection of clinical or biochemical data. Data gathering tasks that can rely on more digital processes, such as retrieving archival documents or text, are less underrepresented, while purely digital data collection tasks, such as collecting online data, can be overrepresented. Ideation and hypothesis generation tasks also have low usage, accounting for 4.2% of sessions on Claude and 2.1% on Claude Code, compared with 7.1% of researcher time.

blocks.text: Comparing observed usage to survey evidence. Along with our analysis of Claude and Claude Code sessions, we conducted a survey of 528 scientists, whose self-reported AI usage lines up with the patterns we observed in those sessions. The sample consists of researchers primarily in the life and health sciences who are active adopters of AI.7 Consistent with the Claude usage patterns shown in Figure 3, survey participants’ self-reported AI usage is highest for data analysis and writing and communication, and lower for ideation and hypothesis generation and data gathering. Participants also report more shared or delegated use of AI for data analysis and writing and communication (Figure 4).

blocks.text: The survey also asked which categories matter most for producing important research results. Respondents rank ideation and hypothesis generation first and data gathering second. Notably, these categories are underrepresented in self-reported usage as well as in Claude sessions. The reasons for this underrepresentation likely differ. Much of data gathering is physical, while ideation is not. For ideation, scientists may prefer generating ideas themselves, or they may perceive AI’s capabilities as limited. Our data may also undercount ideation, since it tends to be woven into many other research tasks and is difficult to classify. But AI may also be genuinely weaker at high-level ideation, such as choosing which research question to pursue and designing a study to answer it.

inlines.text: Biological and biomedical use of Claude Science.

While Claude and Claude Code are general-purpose interfaces, specialized AI tools for the sciences are increasingly available. To study whether such tools support more specialized and demanding research, we use our privacy-preserving analysis infrastructure to compare biology and biomedical work on Claude Science with that on Claude and Claude Code.

blocks.text: Claude Science connects Claude to many research tools and databases that are otherwise fragmented and acts to integrate and accelerate scientific workflows. Scientists must often use different platforms, each with unique data structures or query languages, to combine distinct tools and databases in their research. For example, biologists studying whether existing drugs can act on a specific protein must typically consult separate databases regarding the protein’s function, its structure, compounds already tested against it, and related drug trials or papers. Claude Science combines these into one workflow.

blocks.text: We find that researchers use Claude Science for more specialized tasks than Claude (Figure 5). For example, the task “Propose mechanistic models for protein–protein or protein–ligand interactions” is 5.6x more likely to appear on Claude Science than on Claude. This task involves explaining, at the level of individual molecular contacts, how a protein binds to another protein or to a small molecule such as a drug. Claude Science is well positioned for this task, as it can gather protein structures and binding data from multiple connected databases and combine them into a testable model of the interaction. By contrast, Claude Science is used relatively less for general tasks such as drafting manuscripts or coordinating with collaborators. Moreover, we find that ideation and hypothesis generation accounts for 8% of Claude Science sessions, roughly on par with the share of researcher time these tasks take, suggesting that specialized AI tools for science can facilitate more complex and creative work.

Finally, the artifacts produced with Claude show clear differences across fields (Figure 7).9 Written artifacts such as documents, reports, or academic papers are more common in the social sciences and humanities, relative to the natural and formal sciences. Technical artifacts are about twice as common on Claude Code as on Claude, but the broad pattern across fields is similar (see the Appendix).

blocks.text: Does AI usage track AI capabilities? Field size explains some of the variation in Claude use, but not all of it. For example, researchers in computer science use Claude far more than the field’s size predicts, while those in nutrition use Claude far less. Similarly, where researchers spend their own time does not fully predict where they use Claude the most. Some broad task categories, such as data analysis and writing, have a much larger share of usage than of research time, while others, such as data gathering and ideation and hypothesis generation, have a much smaller share. Here, we test whether these differences in usage reflect what AI can actually do.

blocks.text: To measure task-specific AI capabilities, we first construct capability scores using an LLM classifier. For each task, SciNet provides a list of individual steps that a scientist needs to perform to complete the task. For instance, in chemistry, one task involves purifying reaction mixtures, and one of that task’s steps involves packing a chromatography column. The classifier is shown pairs of steps across the taxonomy and asked which one AI can perform better. We aggregate these comparisons using a Bradley–Terry model—the same model behind the Elo ratings that rank chess players based on head-to-head results. A step’s score rises when it wins comparisons and falls when it loses them. We then average each task’s steps to obtain a task-level score (see the Appendix for details). We label this measure theoretical AI capability. We refer to a task’s specific score as its AI capability score.

blocks.text: To compare usage across tasks, we ask whether Claude use is higher or lower for a task, relative to the time researchers spend on that task. For example, a task that takes 5% of researchers’ time but accounts for 10% of Claude sessions would represent twice as much use as expected, a ratio of 2. A ratio of 1 indicates that Claude use is in line with researcher time spent on the task. A ratio below 1 indicates that Claude is used less than expected based on the amount of researcher time the task takes.

blocks.text: Figure 8 shows that this use ratio rises sharply with a task’s AI capability score. For tasks in the lowest 20% of capability scores, like purifying reaction mixtures and conducting participant observation, Claude is barely used. At median capability scores, the ratio is roughly 1, so usage is in line with researcher time. For tasks in the top 20% of capability scores, like visualizing data and applying statistical tests, usage is about twice as high on Claude and about four times as high on Claude Code, compared with the typical time researchers spend on those tasks. These patterns suggest that scientists’ use of Claude closely tracks AI capability scores. The steeper gradient for Claude Code reflects its focus on computational work, which has higher capability scores.

blocks.text: Consider RL suitability. In RL, an AI model tries a task repeatedly and is rewarded when it succeeds, allowing the model to learn how to perform that task. Tasks are particularly suitable for RL when success is easy to verify, when many examples can be simulated in a computing environment, and when feedback can be delivered quickly (Lambert et al. 2024; Guo et al. 2025). We use task-specific measures from SciNet for these three RL-related components and summarize them in a single index. A task’s capability score is highly correlated with its RL index score, which was classified separately (correlation of 0.78). This suggests that AI is most capable at the research tasks where RL is easiest to apply.

blocks.text: Other important task characteristics concern the nature of the work. Some research tasks are fundamentally cognitive, while others require physical actions or interpersonal contact. Physical tasks in general are beyond the reach of purely cognitive machines. There can also be regulatory restrictions that limit AI use. AI capability scores are higher for tasks characterized by cognitive work (correlation of 0.69). By contrast, research tasks that involve more physical work have lower AI capability scores (−0.57). Scores also tend to be lower for research activities that include interpersonal work (−0.31) or that involve regulatory restrictions on AI use (−0.38).

blocks.text: Research acceleration scenarios with AI

inlines.text: Research acceleration scenarios with AI

blocks.text: The pace of scientific and technological progress depends on good ideas and the means to pursue them. Historically, both have been limited by human capacity. There are only so many researchers, and each has only so much time to formulate a hypothesis, design the right tests, run the analyses, and synthesize the findings.

blocks.text: AI could ease these constraints in two ways. First, it could take on work that researchers now do, allowing them to pursue more ideas. Second, it could contribute ideas that researchers might not otherwise identify. The second may ultimately matter most, but it is much harder to measure, so our analysis focuses on the first.

blocks.text: Approach

inlines.text: Approach

blocks.text: We consider three scenarios of scientific acceleration through AI. Scenario 1 assumes wide adoption of current AI capabilities, as estimated from our survey and the AI capability scores. Scenarios 2 and 3 are hypothetical futures in which AI fully automates 75% or 100% of non-physical research steps—the individual actions that make up each research task in SciNet—starting with the steps that have the highest AI capability scores. In all three scenarios, researchers continue to perform physical steps. These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. They show how physical work, theoretical AI capability, and the cost of AI could shape the acceleration of scientific research, and which fields could accelerate the most.

Scenarios 2 and 3 are hypothetical futures in which AI fully automates 75% or 100% of non-physical research steps—the individual actions that make up each research task in SciNet—starting with the steps that have the highest AI capability scores. blocks.text: For each scenario, we report two measures. The first is the AI share: the fraction of researcher time spent on a study that AI could take on. Given how researchers currently allocate their time, it measures how much human research time AI could free up, and it follows directly from our analyses above. Researchers can redirect that freed-up time to other work, increasing research output. Our second measure, the acceleration, estimates this gain: the increase in research output for a fixed research budget, relative to the research output without AI. It tells us how many more research results the same budget could produce. Freed-up time does not translate one-for-one into more output, both because researchers redirect their effort toward the tasks where AI helps less, and because AI itself has costs.

blocks.text: We build the AI share for Scenario 1 from our survey, which records five levels of AI use: none, assistive, shared, delegated, and autonomous. We assume these levels correspond to AI taking on 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of a researcher’s time for a given task step. Within each task category, we rank task steps by AI capability score. We then assign a level of AI use to each task step, in the same proportions reported in our survey, with the highest levels going to the highest-scoring steps. For ideation and hypothesis generation, for example, 17% of responses report no AI use, and 53% report assistive use. The 17% of ideation task steps with the lowest AI capability scores are therefore assigned no AI share, the next 53% are assigned 25%, and so on up the scale. Because respondents are likely to be heavy AI adopters, we treat their reported use as a proxy for what AI can do today. Finally, we aggregate researcher time freed up by AI from steps to fields (see the Appendix).

blocks.text: To compute the acceleration, we use an ideas production function, a standard economic model of how research inputs, such as researcher time, are turned into research outputs. In this model, a paper requires many research tasks (Jones 2026). The tasks are complementary, such that strength in one cannot fully make up for weakness in another. As AI makes some tasks cheaper, researchers shift their effort toward tasks where AI helps less, thereby easing the bottlenecks that limit the overall gain. For example, researchers could spend more time coming up with new questions or running more physical experiments to expand empirical evidence. We calibrate how much these bottlenecks limit the overall gain using Ahmadpoor and Jones (2019). For AI’s cost, we assume that an hour of AI agent time costs $30, compared with $95 for an hour of a researcher’s time, and that AI runs for 0.2 hours for each researcher hour it saves. These are illustrative assumptions: the AI cost uses today’s public list prices. The smaller these costs, the more research can be done within a given budget and the larger the acceleration, as we discuss below. The Appendix describes the model and assumptions.

blocks.text: Scenario 1: Current capabilities

inlines.text: Scenario 1: Current capabilities

blocks.text: With current capabilities, if adopted widely, AI could take on 27–52% of the researcher time needed to produce a new study, with a median of 38% across fields (Figure 13, left panel). These shares imply research accelerations ranging from 1.35x in the arts, 1.36x in anthropology, and 1.41x in chemistry to 1.96x in computer science and 2.02x in statistics (Figure 13, right panel). Accelerations remain limited because AI work today is mostly assistive or shared rather than autonomous, so researchers still spend substantial time on nearly every step. Even the most AI-ready fields, whose work is almost entirely cognitive, reach only about a 2x acceleration. These estimates assume that AI diffuses widely and that researchers apply it to every step where it is useful today.

blocks.text: Two factors explain most of the differences across fields. The first is physical work, which AI cannot take on without physical integrations. In lab and field sciences such as the agricultural sciences, biomedical sciences, chemistry, and materials science, 38–41% of researcher time goes to physical steps, compared with 4% in the median field. The physical share alone explains about one-third of the variation in the AI share. The second factor is the distribution of AI capability scores within cognitive work. The arts and history spend little time on physical steps (10% and 4%, respectively), yet their cognitive steps have low AI capability scores, perhaps because qualitative and interpretive work is less amenable to reinforcement learning. Computer science and statistics, by contrast, have high scores and large AI shares, driven by data analysis, the type of work with the highest AI capability scores across fields.

inlines.text: Scenarios 2 and 3: Greater automation

blocks.text: In these more speculative scenarios, which depend heavily on assumptions about AI’s reach and costs, greater automation raises both the AI share and the acceleration sharply, and widens the differences between fields.

blocks.text: In Scenario 2, where 75% of non-physical steps can be done by AI, accelerations reach about 8x in computer science, 7x in statistics and library and information science, and 6x in economics. Most other social sciences, mathematics, and physics and astronomy reach 4–5x, while bench and medical sciences reach about 2–3x. The bench sciences and the arts and humanities gain the least, but for different reasons. In the bench sciences, much of the work is physical and must still be done by researchers. In the arts and humanities, the work is mostly cognitive but has low AI capability scores, so few of its steps are among those automated. Automated steps make up 82% of non-physical researcher time in computer science but only 28% in the arts. History, anthropology, and the arts accelerate by about 2x or less.

Once AI automates all non-physical steps, low AI capability scores no longer limit cognitive work, and AI can take on nearly all research work in many fields (Figure 13, left panel). In this speculative scenario, fields with few physical tasks, including statistics, computer science, economics, mathematics, psychology, and most of the social sciences and the arts and humanities, reach about 15–16x. blocks.text: Two lessons follow from these scenarios. First, physical bottlenecks remain powerful. Steps that AI cannot perform without physical integrations come to dominate researcher time and budgets, capping acceleration. Second, where no such bottlenecks exist, extraordinary rates of progress become possible, and AI’s cost becomes the limit. Under our assumptions, a task that is fully automated by AI still costs about one-sixteenth of what it would cost a researcher to perform, so accelerations approach about 16x and stop there. Lower AI costs would raise this ceiling proportionately, such that halving the cost of AI, for example, would double the rate of progress. If costs fall sharply, including for harder tasks that AI automates later, the fields without physical bottlenecks could accelerate far beyond these estimates.

blocks.text: These calculations have important limits that cut in both directions. We do not consider constraints at the level of a field rather than a research team. For instance, only so many experiments can run at facilities like the Large Hadron Collider. We also count only the cost of researcher and AI time, not the costs of machinery or inputs for experiments, which can be substantial in the health, physical, and life sciences. Nor do we consider simulations to replace physical experiments, which could ease bottlenecks in some fields. Finally, we do not consider the quality of ideas. If AI identifies better hypotheses with higher chances of success, research could accelerate further; if research taste remains uniquely human, the acceleration would be slower.

blocks.text: Researcher expectations

inlines.text: Researcher expectations

blocks.text: The scenarios above characterize a range of possibilities. Researchers’ own expectations can provide a unique guide grounded in expertise. To gather their viewpoints, our survey of researchers in the life and health sciences asked when they thought AI, working on its own, would match the best researchers in their field for different categories of research work (Figure 15). Respondents’ expectations are high in the near term: over half expect AI to match top researchers at data analysis by 2027, and 38% say that AI has already reached this level. By 2030, 94% expect AI will match the best researchers in data analysis, 89% in writing, and 72% each in ideation and data gathering. Expectations for ideation and data gathering are lower, consistent with the lower use of Claude for these tasks today.

blocks.text: Expectations for end-to-end AI research without humans in the loop are more conservative, but researchers still expect remarkable progress. About 40% of respondents expect AI to carry out full research projects by 2030, and about 64% by 2035, although 16% say it will never happen. Expectations that AI will autonomously produce scientific breakthroughs are more cautious still, with approximately half of researchers expecting this to occur only after 2035, if ever. Overall, many researchers expect high levels of automation in the next decade, broadly in line with our greater automation scenarios. How fast and to what extent these expectations materialize will depend not only on advances in AI as a software technology, but also on efforts to build automated labs that overcome physical barriers.

blocks.text: Comparing past survey evidence to realized outcomes suggests that AI progress has often been dramatically underestimated (Rosenberg et al. 2026). In a survey in mid-2022, for example, the median estimate for AI achieving gold-level performance in the International Mathematical Olympiad was 2030 among domain experts and 2035 among superforecasters (Karger et al. 2023). AI achieved this milestone in 2025, some five to 10 years ahead of those predictions. While forecasters have systematically underestimated progress in AI capabilities, there are a few exceptions, primarily in domains that require execution in the physical world, such as AI-assisted laboratory tasks in biology.

blocks.text: Discussion

inlines.text: Discussion

blocks.text: If AI helps speed up scientific discovery, it could contribute to higher standards of living and faster progress in treating disease. Our estimates suggest the potential gains are substantial. But advancements in AI’s research capabilities do not automatically translate into rapid progress; achieving such acceleration will also depend on how we respond to several constraints.

Our estimates suggest the potential gains are substantial. But advancements in AI’s research capabilities do not automatically translate into rapid progress; achieving such acceleration will also depend on how we respond to several constraints.

blocks.text: First, adoption can substantially lag capabilities. Diffusion of new technologies is typically slow (Comin and Hobijn 2010), and productivity gains tend to materialize only after organizations restructure around them (David 1990; Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson 2021). Individual learning processes, friction at the organizational or system level, and constraints on AI access or infrastructure can all slow adoption.

blocks.text: Second, research may continue to face bottlenecks that AI does not remove. Physical experimentation, which can be costly and slow, can substantially limit progress even with extremely capable AI. We see this especially in the bench sciences in the scenarios above. Choosing what to study may be another bottleneck. Research questions largely determine a research project’s value, and AI’s capacity to generate good questions remains unclear. If ideation is a bottleneck, it will limit acceleration even as answering a given question becomes much cheaper. Conversely, if AI outstrips humans in formulating high-quality hypotheses, acceleration could be more substantial, especially in domains where testing hypotheses is costly.

blocks.text: Third, AI-enabled research could raise the quantity or quality of research output, with different implications for science. A surge in new research papers could advance a field faster but also overwhelm scientists’ capacity to absorb or verify the results. On the other hand, new technologies, from microscopes and telescopes to statistical software, have historically raised the quality of scientific insights, and AI can likewise make more comprehensive analyses and more ambitious projects feasible. And as papers become easier to produce, the research community may increasingly reward work that is especially novel or high quality. Whether more efficient research leads to greater quantity or greater quality will depend on researchers’ choices and the incentives set by journals, funders, and institutions.

blocks.text: Fourth, the way research is organized may change in ways that are hard to anticipate. As AI becomes more capable and autonomous, AI systems could take the lead in verification, refereeing, and communicating important results, which would ease the absorption problem discussed above. Further in the future, AI research agents might also push the frontiers of science in large communities of their own, independently of humans, using robotics and automated labs. Such autonomous AI research would raise questions about how humans keep track of new knowledge, whether they can understand it, and how it is generated.

blocks.text: Fifth, more autonomous AI systems may increase the challenge of ensuring that AI-driven research remains aligned with human goals. Keeping humans involved in key research decisions, such as which questions to pursue and how to pursue them, may matter for safety and human wellbeing as AI agents become more powerful and creative. Discoveries themselves, or the byproducts of research, can also carry risks, particularly in biology, where the same capabilities that speed up medical advances could also produce dangerous knowledge or materials. In such cases, deliberate checkpoints in the research process may be warranted, requiring us to accept slower progress to reduce risk.

blocks.text: Finally, the work that researchers undertake may change substantially. One effect may be a change in researchers’ job satisfaction. If AI takes over enjoyable or rewarding tasks, satisfaction may fall and fewer people may choose research careers. If AI instead takes over tasks that researchers find tedious, satisfaction may rise. Administrative work is one potential target. In the US, principal investigators on federally funded projects report spending about 44% of their research time meeting administrative requirements rather than doing research (Schneider et al. 2020), and easing this burden could be a large boon, saving time and improving overall satisfaction. Ultimately, the net effect is uncertain and may change as AI’s capabilities evolve. An optimistic view is that AI will expand opportunities for discovery, which is core to what makes research careers rewarding. If science is a voyage into the “endless frontier,” AI may be a new vessel, allowing researchers to travel farther across a vast expanse of research questions and discoveries.
